messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Dentist
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me, Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat, Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit

Vignette:
Priya Krishnamurthy is an eighty-year-old divorced South Asian woman who has practiced dentistry for over five decades, most recently running a part-time consulting practice in a mid-sized American city. She presents for psychological support following a terrorist attack she survived approximately fourteen months ago, and her PCL-5 score of 40 places her in the clinically significant range for PTSD symptomatology.

The attack occurred at a crowded civic ceremony Priya had attended with colleagues from a local dental association. A device was detonated in an adjacent building; Priya was inside the main hall when the blast occurred, and the room rapidly filled with acrid smoke that burned her throat and obscured the exits. In the chaos that followed, a security officer physically restrained her from moving toward what she believed was the nearest door, holding her arm firmly and directing the crowd in a different direction. She could hear sirens converging from all directions — first distant, then overwhelming — while she stood immobilised, unable to see clearly through the smoke, uncertain whether a second device might detonate. She was not physically injured, but she remained pinned against a wall by the press of the crowd and the officer's grip for what felt, to her, like an unbearable length of time before she was led to safety.

In the weeks that followed, Priya found that the world had reorganised itself around that afternoon. The smell of smoke — from a neighbour's fireplace, from a patient's clothing, from the brief char of a candle — would arrive without warning and carry her back into that hall with a vividness that felt less like memory and more like recurrence. Sirens, which in a dental practice setting are not uncommon given the clinic's proximity to a fire station, became nearly intolerable. On more than one occasion she stopped mid-procedure, hands trembling, when an emergency vehicle passed outside. She had come to believe, with quiet but firm conviction, that her body was detecting something real each time — that the sirens and the smoke smell were signals, not echoes. What frightened her most was not the memory itself but the certainty that the danger was not over.

Priya's consulting work brought its own complications. The examination chair places her patients in a position of physical vulnerability, but it is Priya herself who has begun to feel trapped. She is certain that rooms in which she cannot quickly orient herself toward an exit are unsafe, and she now arrives early to every clinical session to identify the nearest door and position herself accordingly. During patient appointments she works with one eye on the hallway. She has not returned to the civic centre district where the attack occurred, rerouting her commute by nearly twenty minutes each day to avoid passing within several blocks of the site. What began as a conscious decision has solidified into something that feels less like a choice and more like a physical impossibility — the idea of driving that route produces a tightening in her chest she interprets as confirmation that the area remains dangerous.

The vigilance has accumulated costs. Colleagues have noticed that Priya seems distracted during case consultations, and one junior associate gently asked whether she was well. She deflected the question, but the exchange stayed with her. Over the months since the attack, she has declined two professional invitations that would have required her to attend large indoor gatherings, and a friendship with a longtime colleague has quietly attenuated because the colleague works near the site she avoids. Priya has not named any of this as loss, exactly — she has framed each withdrawal as reasonable precaution — but she is aware, in a way she finds difficult to articulate, that her world has grown smaller.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment at her clinic when a patient's cologne carried a faint smoky undertone and she found herself unable to complete the appointment, excusing herself to the hallway and standing there for several minutes before she could re-enter the room. She is eighty years old, she told the intake coordinator, and she has worked her entire life. She is not ready to stop. What she hopes for, most simply, is to be able to walk back into her own operatory without scanning the ceiling for smoke.
